title: Ink & Switch Introduces Bijou64: Canonical Variable-Length Integer Encoding for Safe Parsing
gist: Ink & Switch released bijou64, a variable-length integer encoding in which every integer has exactly one valid byte sequence, built by Brooklyn Zelenka to remove signature-malleability bugs from the Subduction sync protocol by construction rather than by validation. It decodes small numbers about twice as fast as LEB128 and large numbers 8-10x faster, but Hacker News critics counter that SIMD-based parsers beat it outright and that its max-length case invites exactly the range-check omission it claims to eliminate.

insights.claim: Ink & Switch's bijou64 is a variable-length integer encoding in which every integer maps to exactly one byte representation, designed specifically to eliminate signature-malleability bugs in the lab's Subduction sync protocol.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Format-level elimination of malleability is directly relevant to anyone building content-addressed or signed distributed systems, where redundant encodings are a live exploit path.
insights.locator: Research lab Ink & Switch published bijou64

insights.claim: The design philosophy behind bijou64 is to remove the validation check that mattered rather than add more checks, making the canonical encoding the only encoding that exists for any value.
insights.speaker: Brooklyn Zelenka
insights.so_what: A generalisable security principle — design formats so the unsafe state is unrepresentable — applicable well beyond varints to any protocol with optional validation steps.
insights.quote: Not by adding more checks, but by removing the one that mattered, and making the format such that, with no canonicality check at all, the only encoding that exists for any given value is the canonical one.
insights.locator: Bijou64 addresses this by making alternative encodings impossible

insights.claim: Bijou64's structure uses direct values for initial bytes 0 to 247 that encode the integer without metadata, and tag bytes 248 to 255 that signal payload length, with each length tier adding a fixed constant offset so lower values cannot be padded into larger byte tiers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The offset-per-tier trick is the concrete mechanism that makes bijectivity work and can be reused in any custom binary framing format.
insights.locator: The design relies on two main structural mechanics

insights.claim: LEB128 splits integers into 7-bit chunks with a continuation bit, which permits multiple valid byte sequences for the same number — zero can be encoded as 0x00 or as 0x80 0x00.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Concrete illustration that a decades-old, widely deployed encoding carries an inherent ambiguity that signature schemes cannot tolerate.
insights.locator: Traditional varints like LEB128 divide integers into 7-bit chunks

insights.claim: Redundant encodings become an attack surface specifically in systems using cryptographic signatures, content addressing, or distributed consensus, because specifications mandate rejecting non-canonical input but developers frequently omit or optimise away those separate validation checks.
insights.speaker: Brooklyn Zelenka
insights.so_what: Identifies the failure mode as human — optional checks get dropped under optimisation pressure — which is why format-level fixes outperform specification-level mandates.
insights.locator: In systems using cryptographic signatures, content addressing

insights.claim: The omitted-canonicality-check bug class is presented as the same root cause behind historic vulnerabilities in PKCS#1 v1.5, GnuTLS, and Bitcoin transaction malleability.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Ties an obscure encoding detail to three well-known high-impact failures, which is the argument that will drive adoption in security-sensitive protocol design.
insights.locator: leading to security flaws similar to historic vulnerabilities

insights.claim: Because bijou64's payload is a contiguous big-endian integer, compilers can reduce decoding to a single load and byte swap, giving roughly 2x faster decoding than LEB128 for small numbers and 8 to 10 times faster for larger numbers on x86 and ARM.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The speed gain comes from eliminating bit-masking and branchy continuation-bit scans — a reminder that branch-free layouts, not clever compression, drive modern parsing throughput.
insights.locator: Because the payload is a contiguous big-endian integer

insights.claim: A critic drawing on BONJSON benchmarking argues bijou64's comparison against scalar decoders is the wrong benchmark, since with SIMD instructions ULEB128 or sentinel values win every time on parallelisation, and even SIMD text parsing would outperform bijou64.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: If SIMD is the real frontier, bijou64's performance pitch is weak and its case rests entirely on the safety argument — which changes who should adopt it.
insights.quote: Testing proved that when you move to SIMD instructions, ULEB128 or sentinel values win every time because of the parallelization opportunities.
insights.locator: One commenter, drawing on benchmarking from the BONJSON format

insights.claim: A critic argues bijou64 narrows the checked boundary surface rather than eliminating runtime validation, because forgetting the range check on the first_byte==255 case and allowing 64-bit wraparound is exactly as plausible a bug as missing LEB128 range checks.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The strongest technical objection: a format that removes 99% of checks can make the remaining 1% easier to forget, which is a net-negative outcome.
insights.quote: Forgetting to do the range check on the first_byte==255 case and just letting it do 64-bit wraparound is exactly as much of a plausible bug as missing range checks on LEB128.
insights.locator: Another commenter, dzaima, questioned the core security claim

insights.claim: Non-canonical varint formats are used deliberately: linkers in WebAssembly and DWARF rely on LEB128 padding of unlinked references so they can patch values in place, so canonicality is not universally desirable.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Bounds the addressable market for canonical varints — toolchain and linker use cases structurally require the ambiguity bijou64 removes.
insights.locator: Additional feedback highlighted that non-canonical formats

insights.claim: The reference bijou64 implementation ships in Rust on crates.io under dual MIT/Apache 2.0 licences with JavaScript wrappers on npm and community ports in Elixir, Go, Perl and Java, plus bijou32 and bijou128 width variants in the specification.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Permissive dual licensing plus multi-language ports at launch is the distribution posture that determines whether a format becomes a standard or stays a lab artifact.
insights.locator: The reference bijou64 implementation is available in Rust
